To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) in the early 2000s analysts' perceptions of corporate social responsibility were shifting from viewing it as an agency cost to viewing it as an indicator of future financial performance; 2) this shift in perception led to a change in the relation between analysts' recommendations and CSR ratings; and 3) the shift was most prominent among the most prestigious analysts.

analysts perceive CSR as a negative agency cost, which leads to more pessimistic recommendations in the early 1900s, while in the later period analysts perceive CSR as being associated with better future financial performance, which leads to optimistic recommendations for firms with higher CSR ratings.

(1) in the early 90s sell side analysts perceived CSR as an agency issue and produced pessimistic recommendations for high CSR firms; (2) over time, the perception of CSR shifted from being an agency cost to being an indicator of future firm success; and (3) the change in the perception of CSR was driven by the analysts of highest status.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how analysts assess the financial implications of CSR and how their perceptions of the relation between CSR and future financial performance shift over time.
the role of CSR ratings in sell side analysts' recommendations and how the relation between the two evolves over time.
how analysts' perceptions of corporate social responsibility affect their investment recommendations.

we show how the institutional logics that underpin CSR evolve over time.
CSR is not only good for society, but also good for business.

we show how the emergence of a new institutional logic (stakeholder) affects analysts' perceptions of corporate social responsibility, and how this in turn impacts analysts' investment recommendations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
analysts' perceptions of corporate social responsibility are not constant.
the relationship between corporate social responsibility and financial performance depends on how analysts perceive the role of corporate social responsibility.
analysts are not immune to the changing institutional logic of the time and that the impact of CSR ratings on investment recommendations is a function of the institutional logic that is dominant.
